Introduction

The COVID-19 pandemic, beginning in March 2020, had a heavy impact on the public transit sector around the globe. Valley Metro saw ridership numbers dip as FY19-20 came to a close. The full impact of COVID era ridership can be seen during FY20-21.
Valley Metro peer agencies have experienced similar dips in ridership.

As we pull away from the peak of the pandemic, or perhaps just adjusting to the “new normal”, Valley Metro and transit agencies around the nation are looking for ways to regroup their rider base. Ridership trends are still significantly lower than pre-pandemic levels.
One possible solution comes by providing high school students with free transit rides.
Benefits of youth ridership

• Academic benefits
    • Minneapolis free fare study in 2013 saw a truancy decrease of 23%
    • GPA 0.28 higher than non-pass holders
    • Access to after school programs, extracurriculars, and tutoring (Fan & Das, 2015)
  • Saves MONEY for families
    • VM 31-day reduced pass is $32
    • $32 x 12 months = $384 annually (https://www.valleymetro.org/fares)
  • Saves TIME for families
    • 10 minutes to/10 minutes from school per day
    • 20 minutes x 180 days = 60 hours per school year
  • Emissions reduction
    • Approximately 0.96 pounds of CO2 per mile in a Single Occupancy Vehicle (EPA.gov)
  • Riders for life
    • 2017 study in the Journal of Planning Education and Research found that people with transit exposure at a young age are more likely to continue transit use in adulthood. (Smart & Klein, 2017)
Other Agencies
Metropolitan Transit System MTS (San Diego, CA)
Partnership between San Diego Association of Governments (SANDAG), Metropolitan Transit System (MTS), North County Transit District (NCTD), and the county of San Diego.
SANDAG Youth Opportunity Pass pilot program for youth 18 and under begins May 1, 2022, thru June 30, 2023.
Funded by an overarching Social Equity Early Action Transit Pilot designed to increase transit equity. (Social Equity, n.d.)
TriMet (Portland, OR)

Access Transit Program provides $700,000 in funding via the Statewide Transportation Improvement Fund (HB2017) legislation. Aims to provide free transit passes for high school students that currently receive free and reduced lunches. (Access Transit, n.d.)
Utah Transit Authority UTA (Salt Lake, UT)

System wide Free Fare February for all riders.

UTA expected to miss out on $2.3 million in fare revenue. Funds were raised in
part by state and local government agencies. Pass partner agencies (colleges, healthcare centers, and large corporations) generated the other half of funds by continuing to pay their subsidy.

21.8% of people surveyed during Free Fare February were new riders. Of that, 12.5% were headed to school.

Saw a significant ridership increase between January and February.
Metropolitan Transportation Authority MTA (New York, NY)
K-12 students receive 3 free rides per school day between 5:30AM - 8:30PM. (Student Metrocards, 2020)
OmniTrans (San Bernardino, CA)

Pilot program providing free rides for K-12 students throughout the system with 50% off micro transit. Began August 2021 and originally set to expire February 2022. The pilot program has recently been extended to the end of the school year on May 31, 2022. (OmniTrans, 2021)
Orange County Transit Authority OCTA (Orange County, CA)
Pilot program providing free rides for kids ages 6-18 began September 2021 and originally set to end February 28, 2022.
The program has since been extended through the end of  summer until September 2022.
This program is funded by a Low Carbon Transit Operations Program grant that aims to lower emissions in disadvantaged areas of California. (Youth Ride Free, n.d.)
Howard County, Maryland
Partnership between county leadership, Howard County Public School System, and Regional Transit Authority (RTA).
Reduction in yellow bus service with an operator transition to the public transit system.
The program began September 2021 and ends in September 2022 (Howard County, 2021)
Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority WMATA (Washington D.C.)
Free rides available to students 5 - 21 years old.
Expires September 2022. (DC Student Ride Guide, n.d.)
Tempe Youth Pass

The city of Tempe implemented the Tempe Youth Pass in 2005. The pass is available to students ages 6 - 18 that live and attend school in Tempe. As with the rest of the Valley Metro system, Tempe Youth Pass boardings sharply declined with COVID.
Since being implemented, students ages 14 - 18 have the highest Youth Pass utilization.
Funding comes from a city-wide sales tax. Between 2005 and 2019 the program's average yearly cost was $320,701.89.
The Tempe Youth Pass is still available to Tempe residents.
Objective
Determine which high school(s) would be a quality choice for a free ride program.
Part 1:
Select one school from each district that demonstrates the highest need. This method would ensure equity among the districts.
Part 2:
Evaluate all schools in the study area to determine the overall highest need. This method would maximize resources.
Methodology

• All maps use the NAD 1983 UTM Zone 12N coordinate system.
  • Districts were initially chosen based on their apparent access to transit.
  • Only public high schools have been evaluated due to the attendance age.

Scoring System
Values extracted from ACS demographics and Valley Metro system data were exported to Excel. In total, 9 metrics were considered:

• Population per square mile
  • % of population ages 10 - 14
  • % of population ages 15 - 19
  • % of population reported as a minority
  • % of population without a high school diploma
  • % of population 150% below poverty
  • % of population without vehicle access
  • Number of bus stops per square mile
  • Miles of service per square mile
Part 1: District Equity
The goal for part 1 was to pick the highest ranking school from each district as the best candidates to receive free fare.
Schools were only evaluated against schools within their own districts.
For every given metric, score ranging from 1 - X were given based on the number of schools in the district. For example, Phoenix schools received a 1 - 10 score while Tempe schools were scored 1 - 6.
Each metric value was arranged in ascending order with an ascending  1 - X score given.
The metric scores for each school were added together for a final school score. The final scores were compared to determine the highest need school for each district.
Part 2: Maximizing Resources

With current constraints such as the cost of gas, general price increases, and labor shortage, part 2 aims to maximize our resources by highlighting the highest need schools throughout the entire study region.
Scoring for part 2 was very similar, however all schools were ranked together, scoring 1 - 41.

Summary

The entire Phoenix and Glendale school districts were discovered as ideal candidates for a free pass program. All of their schools have ample access to transit and demonstrate a high level of need based on demographic factors.
Next Steps

• Contact school districts to determine their interest and present findings.
  • Establish rider criteria and create funding models
    1. Open to all students or those on free/reduced lunch
    2. Year long or semester long
    3. Unlimited access or specified number of trips
  • Determine funding source
    1. Valley Metro is unable to apply for grants
    2. Work with school districts, DES, and/or HUD to secure grant funding
    3. City tax
    4. Funding worked into future transportation plans
    5. Consider reducing yellow bus service to be replaced with transit
    6. Subsidized cost
  • Use Share the Ride to incentivize student ridership
    1. Give away school swag and locally donated gift cards
    2. School/district based competitions
